> **Key takeaways**
> - Use your real business name. Google's rules say no extra keywords in it.
> - One specific main category beats a long list of loose ones.
> - Ask every family for a review, never only the happy ones, and never for a reward.

## Why parents find you here first

When a parent types "swim lessons near me" or "art class for 6 year olds Pasadena", the map results often show up before any website. Those results come from Google Business Profiles. A complete, accurate profile is no promise of a top spot, but a thin or wrong one makes it easy for a parent to pick the studio down the road.

This checklist walks through each part of the profile in the order you will meet it.

## 1. Claim and verify the profile

Search for your business on Google Maps. If a profile already exists, claim it; if not, create one. Google then asks you to verify that you run the business. The method is chosen by Google, not by you: it can be a phone call or text, an email, a live video call, or a postcard, and some businesses have to do more than one. If a video call is offered, Google recommends it. Be ready to show your signage, your space and something that proves you run the business.

## 2. Use your real business name

Google's guidelines say your name should match your real-world name, as used on your storefront, website and paperwork. That means no taglines, no service words and no city names that are not part of your name. "Little Waves Swim School" is fine. "Little Waves Swim School – Best Kids Swim Lessons Glendale" breaks those rules.

## 3. Pick the right category

Google asks you to use as few categories as possible, and to choose ones that finish the sentence "This business IS a…", not "…HAS a…". Pick the most specific main category that describes what most of your families come for. A dance studio that also runs a summer camp is still, first, a dance school. Add a second category only if it is a real, separate part of your business.

## 4. Address, or a service area if you travel

If families come to you, use your exact street address, and make sure the location is staffed during the hours you list.

If you go to them (in-home tutoring, a mobile coding club, a coach who teaches at local parks), you are a service-area business. Google's rules say to hide your address in that case and list the areas you serve instead, kept to roughly two hours of driving at most. A home address should never be shown just because that is where you do your paperwork.

## 5. Hours that match the front door

List the hours families can actually reach or visit you. Before winter break, spring break and summer, add special hours so nobody drives to a locked door. A parent who shows up once to a closed studio rarely comes back to check again.

## 6. Photos: your room, your kit, no children's faces

Add clear, bright photos of the real space: the room, the equipment, the entrance and where to park. Update them when you repaint or rearrange. These do more than stock images, because parents want to picture their child walking in.

Leave children's faces out of public photos unless you have the parents' written permission for that exact use. Kids from behind, hands at work, or an empty room ready for class all show the experience without the risk.

## 7. Reviews: ask everyone, reward no one

Reviews are what most parents read first. Google's review policy says a business may ask customers to share a genuine experience, but must not:

- offer anything in exchange for a review (a discount, a free class, a gift),
- ask only the families you expect to be happy, or discourage negative reviews,
- pressure people to write a review while they are still on site.

A simple habit works: at the end of a term, send every family the same short note with your review link. Then answer each review, good or bad, in a calm, short reply. For a bad one, thank them, say what you will look into, and offer to talk privately. Never share details about a child in a public reply.

## 8. A booking link that goes to your page

If Google shows a booking option for your category, you can add a link to it once your profile is verified. Google's link policy says the link must go to a page for your business, not a general landing page. That can be your own booking page, or your vendor page on ORYN Quest, which shows only your classes and lets families book them.

## 9. Keep it alive

A profile that was set up once and then forgotten slowly goes stale. Put a monthly reminder in your calendar to:

- check your hours and special hours,
- add one or two new photos,
- answer new reviews,
- update your class descriptions for the new term.

Ten minutes a month keeps the profile working for you.

## FAQ

### Can I add "kids classes" to my business name to rank higher?

No. Google's guidelines say the name must match your real-world name, with no extra keywords or service words.

### I teach at local parks and families' homes. Do I show my address?

No. Google treats you as a service-area business: hide your address and list the areas you serve, within about two hours of driving.

### Can I give a discount to families who leave a review?

No. Google's review policy does not allow any incentive for a review, including discounts or free classes. You can ask every family for an honest review.

### Can my booking link point to a marketplace?

Only to a page for your business itself. Google's link policy rules out general landing pages, so link to a page that shows only your classes.
